docs.title: RF Analyzer User Manual
docs.text: Welcome to the RF Analyzer user manual. This guide will help you to install, configure, and effectively use the app for spectrum analysis and signal demodulation.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Real-time FFT & waterfall spectrum visualization
  • Support for RTL-SDR, HackRF, Airspy, Airspy HF+, HydraSDR, rtl_tcp servers, KiwiSDR web receivers and IQ file playback
  • Analog demodulation (AM, FM narrow and wide, LSB, USB, CW) with a squelch relative to the noise floor
  • Adjustable SDR settings (frequency, gain, sample rate, etc.)
  • Adjustable FFT settings (FFT size, averaging, peak hold, frame rate, etc.)
  • Raw IQ and baseband recording and playback
  • Bookmarks for Stations and Bands
  • Import from SDR# or SDR++
  • Automatically synchronize with online lists (EiBi DB, POTA & SOTA Spots)

docs.title: New in RF Analyzer 2.3
docs.text:
• Built-in RTL-SDR driver - no extra driver app needed
  • KiwiSDR web receivers as a source, with a public receiver list and map
  • Quick tune & zoom: long-press the spectrum
  • True dBFS levels, automatic FFT size, smoother waterfall and much lower CPU use
  • Squelch relative to the noise floor, per mode; baseband recording
  • Location-aware band plans and license-free band lists
  • Every USB SDR is recognized when you plug it in; optional start on plug-in and automatic restart after a USB dropout

docs.title: New in RF Analyzer 2.0
docs.text:
• Complete rework of the app in a modern language (Kotlin) and with a modern Material Design based UI
  • Demodulation can run as background service without a foreground app
  • Significant performance improvements
  • Built-in context-aware help and a full offline in-app manual
  • Compatible with the RTL-SDR Blog v4

Refer to the Quick Start section for your first steps.

For information on how to install the app and connect your SDR device look into the Installation & Setup section.

docs.title: About the App
docs.text:
RF Analyzer is an open source spectrum analyzer that lets you use your SDR hardware together with an Android device. A detailed description can be found in the manual.

Changelog: changelog.txt

docs.title: About the author
docs.text:
Hi! I’m DM4NTZ, a ham radio operator and open-source developer.

I'm the creator and maintainer of RF Analyzer, an open-source software-defined radio (SDR) app for Android. The app lets you visualize and analyze RF signals in real time using SDR hardware such as RTL-SDR dongles.

My goal is to make SDR technology more accessible, portable, and open for radio enthusiasts, experimenters, and learners.

As a licensed amateur radio operator, I'm passionate about signal processing, wireless communication, and the broader SDR ecosystem. I also contribute to open-source projects, share knowledge with the ham radio community, and continuously improve my tools based on user feedback.

If you like what I'm building or want to support the development of RF Analyzer and related open-source SDR tools, you can support me with one of the following options. Every contribution helps keep the project alive and open for everyone.

docs.title: Understanding dB, dBm and dBFS
docs.text:
The decibel (dB) is a logarithmic unit used to express ratios - usually power or amplitude ratios - in a compact and human-friendly way. Instead of saying "this signal is 10,000 times stronger than that one", you can just say "it's 40 dB stronger". Decibels are relative by design - you always need to know what the reference point is.

Here are a few common variants:

  • dB: A relative unit without a fixed reference. You’ll often see it used in comparisons like “signal-to-noise ratio = 50 dB”.
  • dBm: This is a power measurement referenced to 1 milliwatt. A signal of 0 dBm means it's 1 milliwatt of power. This unit is useful for real-world measurements and requires proper calibration.
  • dBFS: Short for decibels relative to full scale. It’s used in digital systems, where 0 dBFS is the maximum level that the system can represent. All other values are negative (e.g., -10 dBFS, -40 dBFS), since they are below this maximum.

docs.title: Why the App Uses dBFS, Not dBm
docs.text:
You might expect the signal strength in the app to be shown in dBm, but here’s the catch: dBm requires exact knowledge of the hardware’s RF chain - including gain stages, losses, antenna efficiency, and calibration constants. Every SDR device is different, and many don’t provide accurate power calibration out of the box.

Instead, the app shows signal levels in dBFS - decibels relative to the full scale of the incoming digital signal from your SDR. This is a digital measurement, and it’s consistent across devices because it’s based on the signal’s amplitude relative to the device’s own maximum input range.

What this means for you:

  • The values are still very useful for comparing signal strengths (e.g., “this signal is 20 dB stronger than the noise floor”).
  • However, they are not absolute - you can’t use them to determine whether a signal is actually -73 dBm at the antenna, for example.

docs.title: Understanding the Fast Fourier Transformation
docs.text:
The Fourier Transformation is a powerful tool used throughout signal processing, and it’s at the heart of what your SDR app shows in the spectrum and waterfall displays. In simple terms, it allows us to "look inside" a complex signal and break it down into its individual frequency components.

Imagine you are listening to an orchestra: although all the instruments play together, your brain can often distinguish the violins from the trumpets. The Fourier Transform does something similar for signals - it shows how much of each frequency is present at any given moment.

In practice, we use a computational method called the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT). It's an efficient algorithm that performs the Fourier Transform on discrete digital data. It’s what allows your device to visualize the signal spectrum in real time without needing supercomputers.

docs.title: FFT Size
docs.text:
The FFT size determines how many signal samples are analyzed at once when transforming the signal from the time domain to the frequency domain. This directly affects the frequency resolution - how precisely we can distinguish between different frequencies.

Importantly, frequency resolution depends on both:

  • the FFT size
  • and the sample rate of the input signal.

The formula is simple:

Frequency Resolution = Sample Rate / FFT Size

This means that higher sample rates - like those used with wideband devices such as the HackRF - require larger FFT sizes in order to achieve useful frequency resolution. If you're trying to analyze narrow signals such as SSB (Single Sideband) or CW (Morse code), using a small FFT size with a high sample rate can result in a blurry spectrum where individual signals are difficult to distinguish.

In contrast, if you're using a lower sample rate or analyzing wideband signals (like FM broadcast), smaller FFT sizes may already provide sufficient detail.

docs.title: Ham Radio
docs.text:
Amateur radio, often simply called ham radio, is a globally licensed hobby and service that allows individuals to explore the airwaves, communicate with others across the world, and experiment with radio technology.

Amateur radio operators use specific frequency bands allocated by international agreements. They are allowed to communicate for non-commercial purposes, engage in emergency services, and even bounce signals off the moon or satellites!

Unlike commercial radio or unlicensed bands (like CB or PMR), operating as a ham requires passing an exam and obtaining a callsign. This may sound daunting - but it’s also incredibly rewarding.

Ham radio blends technical learning, practical skills, and a global community. Whether you are interested in voice contacts, Morse code, digital data modes, or just tuning the bands to listen, there’s something in it for everyone.

Learn more:

  • IARU - International Amateur Radio Union
  • ARRL - American Radio Relay League
  • RSGB - Radio Society of Great Britain
  • DARC - Deutscher Amateur-Radio-Club

Want to get inspired? Try tuning into an amateur band using this app. You’ll often hear contacts in progress, and different modes like USB or CW depending on the band.

Best regards (or as we hams like to put it: 73), Dennis (callsign: DM4NTZ)

docs.title: Bookmarks
docs.text:
RF Analyzer offers a comprehensive bookmarking feature which lets the user bookmark various information about stations and bands:

  • Station: The word station is used for a generic RF transmitter or signal. Examples are broadcast radio stations, ham radio operators, ...
  • Band: A band is a frequency range with a description (e.g. a ham radio band)

Station and band bookmarks can be sorted into lists and viewed as list or as overlay elements directly inside the FFT plot. In both cases filtering can be done based on frequency range, mode or search terms. Stations and bands can also be marked as favorites which are quickly accessible from the Bookmark Favorites Dialog.

Additionally, it is possible to access online station lists. Currently supported are:

  • EiBi Database (Shortwave Broadcast Radio Stations)
  • POTA (Parks-on-the-Air) Spots
  • SOTA (Summits-on-the-Air) Spots

docs.title: Bookmark Manager
docs.text:
The Bookmark Manager is the main screen to access all bookmark-related features of RF Analyzer. It can be entered via the Bookmark button which is floating above the control drawer. It is also available from the Bookmark Favorites dialog which can be entered via the button from the demodulation tab.

The screen is divided into three primary pages and a settings page, accessible via the bottom navigation bar:

  • Lists: Logical folders used to group both Stations and Bands. Also contains special Online Lists (EiBi, POTA, SOTA) with automated update settings.
  • Stations: Lists all station bookmarks (including stations from online lists). Can be filtered for lists, online lists, frequencies and more.
  • Bands: Lists all bands.
  • Settings: Configure display of stations and bands inside the FFT. Manage backups, imports and exports of bookmarks.

docs.title: Bookmark Favorites Dialog
docs.text: The Bookmark Favorites Dialog provides quick access to your most important bookmarked stations and bands without leaving the main screen of the app. It displays a list of stations and bands that you have marked with the Heart icon (your Favorites). Tapping a station in this dialog immediately tunes the radio to the stored frequency and applies the saved demodulation settings. Tuning to a station - from here, from its label in the FFT or from the Bookmark Manager - also starts the analyzer if it is stopped and the source is ready (a file chosen, a server set, or the SDR plugged in). Tapping a band moves your viewport to exactly the start and end of the band if your SDR bandwidth (sample rate) supports it.

docs.title: Lists
docs.text: Lists are used to keep your database organized (e.g., "Airband", "Local Repeaters", "Marine", "Amateur Radio Bands", etc.). To display the stations or bands of a specific bookmark list (or online list), use the arrow-button on the right hand side of the list card. This will automatically navigate to the station or band page and select the selected list as filter. Note that other filters (such as frequency range, etc.) are untouched.

docs.title: Create and Edit Lists
docs.text: You can create a new list using the plus icon on the Lists page. Lists are specific to a type: they contain either Stations or Bands, but not both. Lists have a color setting which is applied when displaying stations or bands inside the FFT plot.

docs.title: Actions on Lists
docs.text:
By tapping the three-dot menu on a list card, you can perform the following actions:

  • Delete: Remove the list and all its contents.
  • Edit: Rename the list or change its color.
  • Export: Opens the export sheet for this list: Export saves its stations or bands as a JSON file, Share sends the file to another app. The file keeps the list membership.
  • Copy/Move: Batch process the stations or bands within the list to organize them into a different list.

docs.title: Manage Online Lists
docs.text:
Online lists are displayed as cards in the Lists page. Each card provides the following actions:

  • Manual Download: Trigger an immediate update from the provider's server.
  • Periodic Background Updates: Enable the "Autorenew" toggle and use the slider to set a periodic update interval (e.g., every 24 hours).
  • Clear Cache: Remove downloaded items.

The card also displays the time of the last successful download.

Stations from Online Lists

Stations which were downloaded from online lists are handled like locally created bookmarks. However, they cannot be edited or deleted individually (because this would be overwritten with the next periodic update or manual download). If you want to edit a downloaded station, copy it into another list first.

docs.title: Create and Edit Stations
docs.text:
To create a new station bookmark, either press the floating Plus-Button on the bottom right corner of the station page of the bookmark manager or the action "Add Station Bookmark" from the menu that pops up when you press the bookmark button on the main screen of the app. To edit a station, first expand a station entry by tapping on it once, then press the three-dot menu button on the bottom right corner of the station card. From there choose the option "Edit".

In either case you will get to the "Edit Station" Dialog which has the following sections:

  • Name
  • Favorite Toggle
  • List
  • Station Frequency
  • Demodulation Mode
  • Station Bandwidth
  • Notes
  • Address (incl. Country)
  • Coordinates
  • Callsign
  • Language
  • Squelch
  • Schedule

Note that not all sections are enabled by default for simplicity. You can always add sections from the bottom of the "Edit Station" dialog if they are missing. Sections which are empty are not saved. Some sections require additional explanation:

docs.title: Station Frequency, Bandwidth and Mode
docs.text:
When tuning in on a station, these values will be applied to the demodulation settings. For further information about these parameters refer to:

  • Station Frequency = Channel Frequency
  • Bandwidth
  • Mode = Demodulation Mode

docs.title: Settings from a Station
docs.text:
Tuning to a station moves the view only if the station isn't visible in it.

When you tune to the station, mode and bandwidth are applied for good. The squelch setting below only holds while you stay on the station: the Demodulation tab shows Settings from "…" until you tune away. As soon as you tune away (the channel leaves the station's bandwidth), change the mode or the source, your own setting applies again - so tuning on to other signals never leaves the demodulator silently on the station's value. Tap ✕ on the notice to return to your settings right away; changing the value by hand makes it your own setting.

docs.title: Address
docs.text:
The address section contains a field for the country and the address line of a station. The address line can hold arbitrary text but is meant to be an address which you would find on a map. In case of POTA or SOTA stations it holds the name of the park or summit.

If the station bookmark has an address set, you can view the location on a map by pressing the "Open in Maps" action from the three-dot menu of the station card. Note that this action will only take the address from this section if no Coordinates section is available, otherwise it will use the exact coordinates.

docs.title: Coordinates
docs.text:
In the coordinates section you can enter classic coordinate (latitude and longitude). It is also possible to specify a Maidenhead Locator. Entering either the locator or the coordinates will fill in the other property automatically.

If the station bookmark has coordinates set, you can view the location on a map by pressing the "Open in Maps" action from the three-dot menu of the station card.

docs.title: Call Sign
docs.text: This field is intended to hold an (amateur radio) callsign. In broadcasting and radio communications, a call sign is a unique identifier for a transmitter station. ITU prefix is usually used to identify a country, and the rest of the call sign is an individual station in that country.

docs.title: Squelch
docs.text:
With this section you can specify whether the Squelch Setting will be enabled or disabled when tuning in on this station. The following options are available:

  • Squelch Enabled: The squelch setting will automatically turn on and be set to the specified value when the station is selected and tuned - while you stay on the station (see Settings from a Station).
  • Squelch Disabled: The squelch setting will automatically be turned off when this station is selected (if it was previously enabled), again while you stay on the station.
  • Squelch Section not selected: If the squelch section is not selected, the squelch setting of the demodulator is untouched when selecting and tuning to this station.

The squelch level is specified in dB above the noise floor, so it fits every SDR, gain and antenna. (Bookmarks from before RF Analyzer measured it that way had an absolute level; they get the default of 10 dB.)

docs.title: Schedule
docs.text:
The schedule provides information about when this station is usually active and transmitting. It is mainly used for broadcast radio stations which are imported from the EiBi Database.

Select a start and end time (in UTC) and (if applicable) the weekdays on which the station is active. The bookmark manager contains a filter which lets you only display stations which are actually active at the current day and time. If the schedule is not set (all values empty), it is assumed to be active all the time.

docs.title: Filter Stations
docs.text:
The filter row allows you to narrow down the listed bookmarks:

  • Search: A text search (matches text inside the fields: name, notes, country, language, callsign).
  • Lists: View only specific lists.
  • Frequency Range: View only stations between a specified start and end frequency. You can leave either start or end frequency empty (0 Hz) to create a "higher than" or "lower than" frequency filter.
  • Modulation Mode: Filter for specific modes like "USB" or "NFM".
  • Favorites: Toggle to see only your favorited (hearted) stations.
  • Currently On-Air: Filters based on the stored Schedule and the current time.

docs.title: Create and Edit Bands
docs.text:
Bands represent chunks of the spectrum. The editor allows you to define:

  • Name
  • List.
  • Start Frequency
  • End Frequency
  • Notes
  • Sub-Bands

docs.title: Start and End Frequency
docs.text: These values (in Hz) describe where the band starts and ends. When choosing to view a band bookmark, the screen will be moved so that the start frequency is exactly on the left edge and the end frequency on the right edge of the visible screen in the FFT.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: In the notes field you can put any text that you like to be associated with the band. Note that this field is also searched via the search field in the Band Filter.

docs.title: Sub-Bands
docs.text:
You can divide a band into smaller segments (e.g., the "CW" or "Data" portion of a Ham band):

  • Adding: Enter the name and range in the sub-band editor and press the Checkmark.
  • Editing: Tap an existing sub-band to load its values into the editor.
  • Removing: Use the Trashcan icon to remove a segment.

docs.title: Filter Bands
docs.text: Bands can be filtered by their parent List, their Frequency Range, or their Favorite status. There is also a search field which lets you search for text inside the band name or notes field.

docs.title: Display Stations and Bands in FFT
docs.text:
You can control how bookmarks appear as visual overlays on the waterfall:

  • Show/Hide in FFT: Toggle the visibility of station or band labels in the FFT plot.
  • Custom Filter for FFT: If enabled, you can specify a filter setting for labels in the FFT. This is enabled by default and initialized with an empty filter which means that all bookmarks are drawn as labels in the FFT screen. If the option Custom Filter for FFT is disabled, the filters you set in the Bookmark Manager's station and band screens are automatically applied to the FFT labels.

docs.title: Backup and Restore
docs.text:
• Export Database: Creates a full backup of all your lists, stations, and bands into a single file.
  • Restore: Overwrites your current database with a backup file.

Warning: Data Loss

The restore action is irrecoverable; always create a fresh backup before restoring.

docs.title: Import and Export
docs.text:
With the option Import stations/bands it is possible to import bookmarks from a file. Supported import formats/sources are:

  • RF Analyzer JSON: Import from a JSON file that was created via an export from RF Analyzer.
  • SDR# Frequencies: Import the Frequencies.xml file usually found in the SDR# root directory.
  • SDR++ JSON: Import the frequency_manager_config.json file from the SDR++ root directory.

With the option Import Default Lists, prepared band plans can be imported. The region is preselected from your location ("your location"); tick the lists you want:

  • Amateur Radio Band Plan (IARU band plan for the selected region)
  • License-Free Bands (CB, PMR446/FRS/MURS, GMRS and similar allocations for the selected region)
  • ISM, Maritime and Air Band Plan

A message says which lists were imported.

Finally, if you upgraded from RF Analyzer version 1.13, the option Legacy Import will be available to migrate your old bookmark database into the new system.

docs.title: Import Mode
docs.text:
When importing stations and bands, they must be placed inside a list. The way this is handled can be selected with the Import Mode. This can be set after the imported file was chosen and parsed:

  • Import as is: Import as is. If the imported file contains names of lists for bands and stations, they will be sorted into those respectively. Should a list not yet exist, it is created automatically. Stations or bands without a list name go into the file's list if it holds only one, otherwise into a new list named "Imported (format) date".
  • Import into single list: This mode lets you choose an existing list for stations and another existing list for all bands which are imported. All list information from the imported file are dropped and not used.
  • Import with prefix: Imported stations and bands will be placed into lists as specified in the imported file (just as with option Import as is). But all list names will be prefixed with a tag you can enter.

docs.title: EiBi Database
docs.text:
A highly respected community database for international shortwave broadcasting. It includes station names, languages, and complex seasonal schedules. Teleprinter broadcasts (such as the DWD's weather RTTY) are tuned in USB.

Visit eibispace.de for more information.

For configuration of periodic updates and other general instructions about online lists see Online Lists.

docs.title: POTA Spots
docs.text:
Real-time "spots" for the Parks-on-the-Air program. These bookmarks are dynamic and will update as amateur radio operators move between different parks and frequencies. Enable a reasonable periodic update to keep up with the latest activity and be able to match transmissions from activators to their spot data.

Spots of digital modes (FT8, FT4, RTTY, PSK31, JS8, "DATA") are tuned in USB.

For configuration of periodic updates and other general instructions about online lists see Online Lists.

docs.title: SOTA Spots
docs.text:
Real-time activity for Summits-on-the-Air. Similar to POTA, these entries help you find "activators" transmitting from mountain tops around the world.

For configuration of periodic updates and other general instructions about online lists see Online Lists.

docs.title: Digital Stations
docs.text:
The presets of the digital modes, curated for RF Analyzer: FT8 and PSK31 bands, APRS and HF packet frequencies, Meshtastic, MeshCore and LoRaWAN channels, paging networks, R09 cities, weather RTTY and more - each with the mode, bandwidth and settings it needs. Only the stations for your area are listed (see Location); they change when your country or region changes.

RF Analyzer ships a copy of this list, so it works without a network, and checks for a newer one once a week (the list is maintained on GitHub, where corrections and additions are welcome). This list is only available while the RF Analyzer Digital Extension is installed.

For configuration of periodic updates and other general instructions about online lists see Online Lists.

docs.title: Demodulation Tab
docs.text: Once you're receiving signals with your SDR or replaying an IQ file, the Demodulation Tab allows you to actually listen to and fine-tune a specific signal. This is where you select the demodulation mode (like AM or FM), adjust demodulation parameters and the audio level.

docs.title: Demodulation Mode
docs.text:
Picking the correct demodulation mode is absolutely essential. If you're not using the right mode for a given signal, the result will be distorted audio — or just static. The demodulator is responsible for decoding how the original audio or data is embedded in the radio signal, and using the wrong one is like trying to play a vinyl record with a laser pointer — you won’t get music, just noise.

Tap the Demodulation Mode button at the top right: a dialog lists the modes with their full names and what they are typically used for, and switches demodulation off at the top. The modes are:

  • AM - Amplitude Modulation
  • FM (narrow) - Narrow-band Frequency Modulation
  • FM (wide) - Wide-band Frequency Modulation
  • LSB - Lower Side Band Modulation (Single Side Band - SSB)
  • USB - Upper Side Band Modulation (Single Side Band - SSB)
  • CW - Continuous Wave (or more commonly: Morse Code)

Each mode is used in different parts of the spectrum, and often the modulation type can be guessed by frequency (use a band plan) or visual signature in the FFT/waterfall. See section Choosing the Right Demodulation Mode for more information.

docs.title: Audio Controls
docs.text:
• Speaker Icon - Tap to mute or unmute the audio output.
  • Volume Percentage - Tap the number to bring up a volume slider

docs.title: Channel Frequency
docs.text:
The channel frequency determines at which frequency the demodulator operates. This is different from the source frequency which selects the center of the captured spectrum. The channel frequency may be chosen anywhere inside the received signal spectrum which is centered around the signal frequency (plus/ minus half of the sample rate in Hz)

There are several ways to set the channel frequency:

  1. Typing directly into the frequency textbox. The textbox is set to insert mode which means it is possible to just type over the current value. Pressing enter on the keyboard or the Apply button sets the new frequency.
  2. Using the tuning wheel below the textbox - swipe or fling the wheel left or right. It moves in steps of the Tune Step slider below it, which each mode remembers on its own (e.g. 9 or 10 kHz for AM broadcast, 12.5 kHz for NFM channels). (Note: the direction of the wheel can be reversed via the Reverse Tuning Wheel setting if desired.)
  3. Dragging the channel selector at its yellow drag button in the FFT view.

Quick Tuning

The tuning wheel is great for small frequency changes. For larger jumps, it's faster to type the frequency or drag the selector in the FFT plot. It is possible to type a frequency which lies outside of the currently received spectrum. RF Analyzer then automatically retunes the SDR if possible.

docs.title: Zoom and Bandwidth
docs.text:
• Zoom - Adjust how wide or narrow the FFT/waterfall viewport appears relative to the bandwidth of the source spectrum. With the slider all the way to the left, the entire spectrum which is received from the SDR is visible. Sliding to the right will zoom in around the channel frequency.
  • Channel Bandwidth (kHz) - Defines how much of the signal bandwidth around the channel frequency should be demodulated. This affects both audio clarity and how much noise or neighboring signals are picked up. The bandwidth can also be changed by sliding the white drag handle in the FFT view. Each mode has its own range and remembers its bandwidth: AM 3 - 20 kHz, FM (narrow) 5 - 25 kHz, FM (wide) 30 - 95 kHz, LSB/USB 1.5 - 5 kHz, CW 0.1 - 0.6 kHz.

docs.title: Squelch Control
docs.text:
The Squelch mutes the audio while no signal is in the channel, like the squelch of a handheld radio. It is available for the analog modes and disabled by default. Each mode keeps its own squelch: on or off, and its level (0 to 40 dB above the noise, 10 dB by default).

The squelch level is set in dB above the noise: RF Analyzer measures the noise floor next to the channel all the time, so the same setting works with every SDR, gain and FFT size - also near the edge of the received band and in a recording that holds only part of its band (10 dB is a good start; lower opens on weaker signals, and on noise if too low). The squelch opens as soon as the channel is that much above the noise, and closes only when the channel has stayed a few dB below that for a moment - it doesn't flutter on a signal near the threshold and doesn't cut off the end of a transmission. The beginning of a transmission, from before the squelch noticed it, isn't lost either.

Once enabled, the squelch line appears in the channel selector of the FFT plot, labeled with the level ("+10 dB"). It follows the noise floor in steps of about a decibel. Slide its drag handle up or down to change the level. The line is green while the squelch is open and red while it is closed.

The level is measured on the channel's own side for single sideband (USB above, LSB below the channel frequency).

The squelch can also be used to automatically start and stop the recorder (see Recording Options).

When you tune to a bookmarked station that stores a squelch, its setting holds while you stay on the station: the tab shows Settings from "…" until you tune away. Tap ✕ to return to your own settings right away.

If your device can't keep up with the processing, the tab shows Overload – samples dropped; tap ? for help (see Processing Overload).

docs.title: Choosing the Right Demodulation Mode
docs.text:
Here are multiple ways to figure out which demodulation mode to use:

  1. By frequency range (check band plans) Many radio services operate on fixed frequency bands and are known to use specific modulation types. Amateur radio, airband, FM radio, etc. all have well-defined standards. Amateur radio bands and other services often have published band plans. These are useful for identifying what mode to expect at a given frequency.
    • IARU Band Plans (Amateur Radio)
    • US FCC Frequency Allocations
  2. Look at the FFT and waterfall display Different modes have distinctive shapes and behavior in the spectrum display. See the examples below for visual cues.

docs.title: AM - Amplitude Modulation
docs.text:
Used for:

  • Shortwave broadcasts
  • Aviation (airband)
  • Some CB radio

Typical bandwidth: 6-10 kHz

Visual signature:

  • Symmetrical peaks around a center frequency
  • Fixed bandwidth

docs.title: Narrow FM - NFM
docs.text:
Used for:

  • Ham radio voice (VHF/UHF)
  • Public safety and utility comms
  • Marine VHF

Typical bandwidth: 12.5-25 kHz

Visual signature:

  • Single peak with a flat top
  • Steady, narrow trace in the waterfall
  • Little or no visible sidebands

docs.title: Wide FM - WFM
docs.text:
Used for:

  • Commercial FM radio (88-108 MHz)

Typical bandwidth: 100-200 kHz

Visual signature:

  • Broad, dense signal
  • Highly modulated (busy waterfall)
  • Often accompanied by strong stereo pilot tone (~19 kHz)

docs.title: USB - Upper Sideband
docs.text:
Used for:

  • Ham radio SSB above 10 MHz
  • Voice on HF maritime and aeronautical bands
  • Audio (de-)modulation of digital modes such as FT8 or PSK31

Typical bandwidth: 2.4-3 kHz

Visual signature:

  • Only the upper side of the carrier is visible
  • Sharp edge on the lower side
  • No center peak (carrier suppressed)

docs.title: LSB - Lower Sideband
docs.text:
Used for:

  • Ham radio SSB below 10 MHz

Typical bandwidth: 2.4-3 kHz

Visual signature:

  • Only the lower side of the carrier is visible
  • Sharp edge on the upper side
  • No carrier spike

docs.title: CW - Continuous Wave / Morse Code
docs.text:
Used for:

  • Ham radio

Typical bandwidth: ~100 Hz

Visual signature:

  • Single sharp carrier wave which is switched on and off
  • Morse Code pattern is visible in waterfall (dashes and dots)

docs.title: Further Resources for Signal Identification
docs.text:
If you're unsure about the type of signal you're observing, the following resources can assist you in identifying various RF signals, including analog audio:

  • Signal Identification Wiki A comprehensive community-driven guide featuring audio samples and waterfall images for a wide range of signals: sigidwiki.com

  • HFUnderground Signal Identification Focused on HF and MW bands, this wiki includes detailed entries with mode, frequency, bandwidth, and visual characteristics: hfunderground.com

  • Tektronix eGuide to RF Signals Offers insights into interpreting spectrograms and understanding signal behavior over time: Tektronix eGuide to RF Signals

  • Understanding the RF Spectrum - Visual Guide A YouTube video that provides a visual walkthrough of the RF spectrum and common signal types. Watch on YouTube

docs.title: Wrapping Up
docs.text:
Now you are able to demodulate audio signals. Developing a good intuition of recognizing signal modulation settings by analyzing the FFT and waterfall comes naturally with time! A good way to practice is to record a brief period of IQ samples on an Amateur Radio band and replay it in a loop. Then it is easy to experiment with the various demodulation settings.

Continue on to Recording.

docs.title: Display Tab (FFT & Waterfall Settings)
docs.text: The Display tab lets you customize how the FFT (spectrum) and waterfall plots are rendered. If you are new to signal processing, have a look at section Understanding the Fast Fourier Transformation for more information about the FFT. These plots are essential for visualizing RF activity and identifying signals. The Display tab is all about tailoring the FFT and waterfall display to suit your needs, whether you're scanning for faint signals or adjusting for smoother performance on limited hardware.

docs.title: Scale of Vertical Axis
docs.text:
This setting defines the dB range shown in the FFT and waterfall displays. It can be used to adjust the vertical scaling and offset. Use it to adapt the view to the strength of the incoming signal. Usually it is recommended to set the lower limit just below the noise floor of the signal and the upper limit a bit higher than the strongest signal. This maximizes the contrast in the waterfall display.

Tip

The vertical scale can also be adjusted via scroll or zoom gestures on the vertical grid area on the left of the FFT plot.

Use Autoscale to automatically adjust the range based on the current signal.

Use Reset Scale to return to a default range.

The range is remembered per source type: signal levels differ between SDRs (and antennas), so switching from e.g. an RTL-SDR to a HydraSDR brings back the range last used with the HydraSDR.

About the dB Unit

The vertical axis of the FFT shows the signal strength relative to the maximum value which is supported by the device. It is measured in dBFS: a sine wave at the full input range of the SDR reads 0 dB, independent of the FFT size and padding. The noise floor, however, depends on the FFT size: a larger FFT spreads the noise over more (narrower) bins, so it is drawn lower, while a narrowband signal stays at its level. Additional information about this can be found in the section Understanding dB, dBm and dBFS.

Zoomed out

When the FFT has more bins than the screen has pixels, each pixel shows the strongest bin it covers. That keeps narrowband signals visible when zoomed out, and lets the noise floor appear a few dB higher than when zoomed in.

docs.title: FFT Size
docs.text:
Controls the number of frequency bins used for the FFT (Fast Fourier Transform).

Larger FFT sizes (e.g., 32768) provide finer frequency resolution but require more samples for each FFT frame which means it causes an averaging effect in the time domain. For small sample rates, a high FFT size will cause the waterfall to look smooth even though there are signals which change rapidly. If you want to see quick changes in signals choose a lower FFT size. Additionally, higher FFT sizes require more RAM for the storage of the waterfall diagram which might cause issues on old devices.

Background Info: FFT Performance

The FFT operation is done in Native Code which is very fast even for large FFT sizes. The restriction for the maximum FFT size is rather the memory usage for the waterfall plot. On very old hardware you might experience crashes related to Out-of-Memory issues. In this case reduce the FFT size or enable the Low Performance Mode.

docs.title: FFT Padding Ratio
docs.text:
At low sample rates, a large FFT size (needed for fine frequency resolution) means each FFT frame spans a long stretch of real time, which shows up as blur along the time axis of the waterfall. FFT Padding Ratio lets you reduce that blur without sacrificing the number of frequency bins: it shrinks the number of real samples analyzed per frame and fills the rest with zeros (up to 75%), so each waterfall row represents less real time.

This is not free: the true ability to distinguish two closely-spaced signals (frequency resolution) is governed by how many real samples are analyzed, not by the number of bins shown, so a higher padding ratio trades some of that resolution for a sharper time axis. The number of bins itself, and thus how smooth the frequency axis looks, stays unchanged.

docs.title: Manual FFT Size
docs.text:
By default, FFT Size and FFT Padding Ratio are chosen automatically from the current sample rate and the Waterfall Speed:

  • Each FFT frame analyzes the samples of one waterfall row (sample rate divided by the waterfall speed). Nothing between two rows is skipped and nothing is smeared over several rows, and the frequency resolution is the finest the waterfall speed allows (about 50 Hz at 30 rows per second). A slower waterfall therefore gives a finer frequency resolution.
  • Above 30 rows per second the frames keep the length of a 30 rows per second row and overlap, so a faster waterfall stretches the time axis (e.g. to see the bits of an RTTY signal) without making the frequency resolution coarser.
  • At low sample rates (e.g. 12 or 48 kSps) the frames are kept longer than one row, so that narrowband signals stay sharp.
  • The FFT size zero-pads the frame by at least 1.5x, which keeps zoomed-in views smooth.
  • At high sample rates the FFT size is limited by the memory and speed of the device (up to 131072 on devices with a large memory budget). Above 60 rows per second the limit gets smaller as the waterfall gets faster, to keep the CPU load in check.

Enable Manual FFT Size to take direct control of both values yourself; the sliders will initially show whatever was last chosen automatically, so you can fine-tune from there.

When Low Performance Mode is enabled, the automatically chosen FFT size is limited to 16384 to ease CPU and memory load on older devices.

docs.title: Max Frame Rate
docs.text:
Limits how often the FFT and waterfall plots are redrawn per second. This does only affect the drawing of the FFT (and waterfall) frames. The rate at which FFT frames are calculated from the input samples is controlled via the Waterfall Speed.

Higher frame rates (up to 60 FPS) make the display smoother, especially when scrolling and zooming.

Lower values reduce CPU and battery usage. The default is 60 FPS; the Low-Performance Mode limits drawing to 30 FPS.

docs.title: Averaging
docs.text:
Smooths out short-term fluctuations of the FFT plot by averaging multiple FFT frames. The setting controls how many FFT results are averaged. The waterfall keeps showing the individual frames.

A value of 0 disables averaging.

docs.title: Waterfall Speed
docs.text:
Adjusts how fast the FFT frames are calculated (measured in frames per second, i.e. fps). The actual speed (FPS) at which the frames are calculated are gated by the speed of the processor of the Android device. Unless Manual FFT Size is enabled, the FFT size follows the waterfall speed (see Manual FFT Size).

Show actual FFT FPS

The actual FFT FPS value can be displayed by enabling the option Show Debug Information.

docs.title: Peak Hold
docs.text:
When enabled, this shows small yellow dot indicators above the FFT curve marking the highest observed signal strength at each frequency.

Useful for spotting intermittent or transient signals.

docs.title: Relative Frequency
docs.text:
When enabled, the spectrum and waterfall plots are centered around the current tuned frequency of the SDR (shown as 0 Hz), showing offsets in ±kHz rather than absolute frequency.

Turn this off if you prefer absolute frequency display.

docs.title: Spectrum/Waterfall Ratio
docs.text:
Adjusts how much vertical space is given to the spectrum plot vs. the waterfall display.

Move the slider right for more spectrum, left for more waterfall.

docs.title: Waterfall Color Map
docs.text:
Choose how the waterfall color gradient maps to signal strength.

Available color maps are:

  • Jet
  • Turbo
  • GQRX (Color Map from the GQRX application by Alexandru Csete OZ9AEC)

Try different maps to see which one suits your eyes and environment best.

docs.title: FFT Drawing Type
docs.text:
Determines how the FFT (spectrum) is drawn:

  • Line: A connected curve.
  • Bars: Fills the space under the curve.

Line mode is the default and typically recommended and a bit more efficient during rendering.

docs.title: Wrapping Up
docs.text: You should now be able to configure the FFT and Waterfall Plot to your liking. If you spot an interesting signal, continue with the Demodulation Tab to demodulate and listen to the signal.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
The following YouTube video explains how to set up your SDR with RF Analyzer:

Alternatively, follow these steps to get started quickly:

  1. Install the app from Google Play Store: RF Analyzer for Android
  2. Connect your SDR device:
    • For USB SDRs (RTL-SDR, HackRF, Airspy, Airspy HF+, HydraSDR) → use a USB-OTG adapter.
    • No SDR? Connect to a public KiwiSDR web receiver (KiwiSDR (web) → Choose from Public List in the next step), or replay an IQ file (File Source).
    • More information about connecting the SDR device can be found under Installation & Setup
  3. In the app navigate to the Source Tab (see SDR Source) and select your source type from the dropdown menu.
  4. Set a tune frequency and initial sample rate, as well as gain values and other source settings (optional; see SDR Source for more explanation on these settings).
  5. Press the play button to start the sampling.
    • First time usage: Grant USB permissions when prompted.
    • You should now see a FFT and waterfall plot.
    • Scroll horizontally to automatically retune the source and find signals in the spectrum.
    • Use pinch-to-zoom gestures to zoom in on signals.
  6. Go to the Demodulation Tab (Demodulation), tap the mode button and select a demodulation mode.
    • Align the channel selector with a signal.
    • Adjust squelch (and potentially the gain of your source).
    • You should hear the demodulated audio signal

Please have a look at the following sections to learn more about all elements of the UI, SDR Source Tab, Display Tab (FFT settings) and demodulation settings, signal recording, bookmarks and more. If you have trouble with the app, have a look at the troubleshooting section!

I wish you a lot of fun analyzing the RF spectrum! :)

docs.title: Recording
docs.text:
The Recording feature allows you to capture IQ (In-phase/Quadrature) data: either the raw samples of your SDR, or the demodulator's baseband (just the channel). The data is saved in a file, which can later be replayed using the File Source in the Source tab or exported for analysis in other tools.

A recording keeps running in the background, also when you swipe RF Analyzer away; the notification then offers Stop recording. If RF Analyzer is closed while a recording runs (force-stopped, or after a crash), it asks at the next start whether to keep the unfinished recording or delete it.

docs.title: View Recordings
docs.text: Press the View Recordings button to open a list of all saved recordings (see Recording List).

docs.title: File Name
docs.text: Use this text input to name your recording. You can enter or update the file name even while the recording is in progress. The name will only be applied when the recording is stopped.

docs.title: Record Raw IQ / Record Baseband
docs.text:
Two buttons start a recording; press the running one again to stop it. Only one of them runs at a time.

  • Record Raw IQ writes the samples of the source as they arrive: the whole received bandwidth at the source's sample rate (large files - an RTL-SDR at 2 MSps writes 4 MB per second).
  • Record Baseband writes only the demodulated channel: complex 32-bit float samples (.cf32) at the mode's baseband rate (e.g. 192 kSps for WFM, far less for narrow modes), centred on the channel frequency. It needs a demodulation mode, follows the squelch in analog modes, and the channel frequency stays where it is while it runs.

While a recording runs, the button shows how long it has been running, and the FFT display shows its frequency, sample rate and current file size with a red dot.

docs.title: Channel Squelch
docs.text:
Toggle this switch to record only while the squelch is open. Each signal is recorded completely: with a little of what came before it (the squelch notices a signal only shortly after it began) and a short tail after it - so digital packets in a squelch-gated recording stay decodable. The recording holds the signals one after another, without the pauses between them. A baseband recording (Record Baseband) of an analog mode follows the squelch whenever the squelch is on.

Note that this option is only available if the Squelch setting in the Demodulation Tab is enabled.

Recording based on squelch is especially useful to avoid storing long periods of silence.

docs.title: Stop Recording After
docs.text:
This setting lets you define an automatic stop condition for the recording. You can choose one of the following limits:

  • Seconds
  • Minutes
  • Megabytes
  • Gigabytes
  • Disabled (default; manual stop required)

Once the selected condition is met, recording will stop automatically.

At the bottom of the tab, the app also displays how much device storage is currently used by recordings.

Warning

Keep an eye on available storage space. Raw IQ recordings can grow large quickly, especially at higher sample rates. Recordings can be deleted from the Recording List.

docs.title: Recording List
docs.text: View the recording list by pressing the View Recordings button in the Recording Tab (or in the Source Tab when File Source is selected).

docs.title: Filter and Delete All
docs.text:
In the top right corner of the recording list are two buttons:

  • Filter Favorites: When enabled, only recordings which are marked as favorite are displayed
  • Delete All: This button deletes all recordings.

The recording list shows all recordings as cards displaying the following information:

  • Recording Name (bold)
  • Tune (Center) Frequency (Hz)
  • Sample Rate (Sps)
  • File Format (RTLSDR, HACKRF, AIRSPY, AIRSPYHF or HYDRASDR; baseband recordings are AIRSPYHF, a KiwiSDR's raw recordings HYDRASDR)
  • Date and Time
  • File Size

Tap a recording card to reveal the following actions:

  • Replay Recording (via File Source)
  • Rename Recording
  • Delete Recording
  • Share Recording File
  • Download Recording File to Folder
  • Mark Recording as Favorite

File Format

Record Raw IQ stores the samples in the SDR's own format - the same as rtl_sdr, hackrf_transfer and similar tools write (a KiwiSDR's as 16-bit IQ). Record Baseband stores 32-bit float IQ (.cf32). The file name holds start time, name, format, frequency and sample rate, e.g. 20261113-012148_My Recording_RTLSDR_97MHz_1MSps.cu8.

Import Recordings into SDR#

SDR# uses the WAV Fileformat. There are converters for the raw IQ files to the SDR# WAV format. A python converter script for HackRF IQ files is available in the Tools directory of the RF Analyzer GitHub Repository. For RTL-SDR IQ files there is a tool called iqtosharp.

docs.title: Wrapping Up
docs.text: Now you are familiar with most of RF Analyzer's features. What's left is the Settings Tab where you can tweak some parts of the app to your preferences and the About Tab where you find this manual, what you purchased, and the options to purchase RF Analyzer.

docs.title: Source Tab
docs.text:
The Source Tab is where you choose and configure the signal input. Before you can analyze signals, you need to select a source type and start the analyzer.

Starting the Analyzer

The Start Button (▶️) is located to the right of the source type dropdown menu. After selecting a source, tap this button to start sampling and display the FFT and waterfall plot.

Most settings can be changed while the analyzer is running, but there are some exceptions, especially for file playback.

docs.title: Selecting a Source
docs.text:
The Signal Source dropdown in the Source Tab lets you choose between different signal sources:

  • RTLSDR - Receive live radio signals using an RTL-SDR USB dongle, or an rtl_tcp server in the network.
  • HACKRF - Works similarly to RTL-SDR but supports wider bandwidths.
  • AIRSPY - A high quality SDR supporting 12bit resolution and up to 10MHz bandwidth.
  • AIRSPYHF - The Airspy HF+: HF and VHF (0.5 - 260 MHz) at up to 768 kSps.
  • HYDRASDR - A high quality SDR supporting 12bit resolution and up to 10MHz bandwidth.
  • KiwiSDR (web) - Connect to a remote KiwiSDR receiver over the network instead of using local hardware.
  • File Source - Replay a previously recorded IQ file.

Automatic Source Detection

When you plug in an SDR (RTL-SDR, HackRF, Airspy, Airspy HF+ or HydraSDR) while the app is in the foreground - or plugged it in while the app was in the background - the correct source type is set automatically.

docs.title: Start/Stop Button
docs.text:
The play button in the upper right starts and stops the signal analyzer. When started, the app begins receiving and displaying IQ samples from the source. Once started, the analyzer keeps running when the app is moved into the background, as long as it demodulates or records (otherwise it stops after a few seconds). A notification icon is displayed in the status bar. Tap the notification to bring the RF Analyzer app back into the foreground or use the Stop button in the notification to stop and terminate the app.

Swiping RF Analyzer away from the recent apps closes it and stops the analyzer - except while a recording runs: the recording goes on, and a notice says so and offers Stop recording.

Each source type changes the available settings. Let’s go over them one by one. We start with some settings that are common to most of the source types:

docs.title: Tune Frequency
docs.text:
This field sets the center frequency (in Hz) to which the SDR device should tune. You can input the frequency manually. The app does also automatically adjust the tune frequency when the Channel Frequency is set to a value outside of the current signal range. Scrolling outside of the current signal also causes an automatic retune of the device.

Info

The app limits the frequency values to the range of the connected SDR. The RTL-SDR is not limited (0 Hz to 3 GHz), because dongles differ so much; if the tuner chip can't receive the chosen frequency (e.g. below 24 MHz without a Blog V4's upconverter or direct sampling), RF Analyzer says so once.

docs.title: Sample Rate
docs.text:
When Automatic Sample Rate is disabled, the dropdown lets you choose the fixed sample rate manually.

By default, Automatic Sample Rate is enabled. The sample rate automatically follows the zoom level of the spectrum display. This provides an intuitive way to adjust bandwidth without needing to manage sampling directly. However, the adjusting of the sample rate does affect the signal which is received from the source which might be undesirable.

docs.title: Gain Controls
docs.text:
Depending on the specific SDR device there are multiple gain controls available. These sliders allow you to optimize the signal level by adjusting different gain stages.

Note that excessive gain may cause distortion or clipping in case of very strong signals.

docs.title: LNA Gain
docs.text: Adjusts the Low Noise Amplifier gain at the RF stage. Sometimes this is also just referred to as 'Gain'.

docs.title: VGA Gain
docs.text: Controls the Variable Gain Amplifier (VGA). Useful for fine-tuning the baseband signal level before digitization.

docs.title: Mixer Gain
docs.text: Adjusts the Mixer gain at the conversion stage from radio frequency (RF) to intermediate frequency (IF).

docs.title: IF Gain
docs.text: Only available with an External RTL-SDR Server whose dongle has an E4000 tuner chip; the built-in driver has no separate IF gain. It allows the fine-tuning of the intermediate frequency (IF) gain.

docs.title: Antenna Port Power
docs.text:
This is sometimes referred to as Bias Voltage, Bias Tee or RF Bias. It enables a power supply on the antenna port of the SDR. This is useful for powering active antennas or external devices requiring a bias voltage.

  • HackRF: 3.3V (max 50mA)
  • RTL-SDR with a bias tee (e.g. Blog V3/V4): 4.5V (max 50mA) - not with an External RTL-SDR Server, whose protocol can't switch it
  • Airspy: 4.5V (max 25mA)
  • HydraSDR: 4.5V (max 25mA)

Warning

Not all devices or antennas are compatible. Use caution to avoid damaging external equipment.

docs.title: Frequency Converter Offset
docs.text:
If you are using an upconverter or other frequency-shifting hardware, enter the offset (in Hz) here. This value (which can be negative) is added to the tuned frequency to display the actual RF frequency.

This feature helps when using hardware like an up-/downconverter that shifts the spectrum into a different frequency range.

Example: Ham-It-Up

For the Ham-It-Up converter the frequency offset setting should be set to -125000000Hz. That means that the app will display the incoming signals as if they were 125MHz lower than they actually are. Now when tuning the app to 14MHz you see the signals that are actually incoming at 139MHz (this is where the 14MHz band is found after up- converting it with the Ham-It-Up converter).

docs.title: RTL-SDR Specific Settings
docs.text: All of the following options can be adjusted while the Analyzer is already running.

docs.title: Hardware AGC
docs.text: Activate the RTL-SDR's built-in automatic gain control. This is not usually recommended as it will add too much noise to the signal.

docs.title: Manual Gain
docs.text: Enable this switch to set the Gain manually (and the IF Gain with an rtl_tcp server that offers it), otherwise the RTL-SDR sets it automatically. Refer to the Gain Controls section for more information about the specific gain stages.

docs.title: External RTL-SDR Server
docs.text:
Connect to an RTL-SDR network server instead of a local USB device. This must be done before starting the analyzer. Input the IP and TCP port of the rtl_tcp server and start the analyzer to connect. Make sure the Server is not blocking the connection with a firewall.

On Android 17 and newer, a server in your local network (for example 192.168.1.20 or raspberrypi.local) needs RF Analyzer's local network access: RF Analyzer asks for it when you start the analyzer. Android lists it under Nearby devices. If you denied it, allow it in the app's settings (Permissions → Nearby devices) - without it the connection times out. Servers on the internet don't need it.

The samples arrive over the network in bursts (rtl_tcp sends a quarter megabyte at a time - half a second at 250 kSps), so the audio plays a little behind the spectrum: RF Analyzer keeps enough audio in reserve to bridge the gaps between bursts. If the audio breaks up, it enlarges the reserve (up to one second); it starts small again with the next start of the analyzer. The same applies to a KiwiSDR.

Warning

Streaming IQ samples from a remote RTL-SDR onto your phone does consume a very high amount of data volume (~4MB/s)! It is highly recommended to do that only over a WiFi connection and not over a paid data plan.

docs.title: Frequency Correction
docs.text: This setting is passed to the RTL-SDR driver and allows to compensate for small frequency offsets due to hardware imperfections. The value has the unit PPM (parts-per-million) and can also be negative.

docs.title: Direct Sampling Mode
docs.text:
Experimental Feature

This feature is experimental. Use at own risk.

Direct Sampling Mode can be used to extend the tunable range for the RTL-SDR device and receive shortwave signals (0 - 28.8MHz).

However it needs a hardware modification of the RTL-SDR. Some RTL-SDR devices already have the modification built in (e.g. the RTL-SDR Blog V3 or the NooElec V5). Choose I-Branch or Q-Branch depending on the modification (the RTL-SDR Blog V3 uses Q-Branch); Off uses the tuner. For more information visit the following link: Direct Sampling Mode (rtl-sdr.com)

docs.title: HackRF Specific Settings
docs.text:
When HACKRF is selected as the signal source, a range of hardware-specific settings becomes available.

The HackRF has two gain stages (LNA and VGA) which are explained in the Gain Controls section. Additionally, it features an amplifier:

docs.title: Amplifier
docs.text: This switch enables or disables the 11dB internal RF amplifier in the HackRF. This is an additional gain stage and may be helpful when receiving very weak signals, though it can introduce distortion if overused.

docs.title: Airspy Specific Settings
docs.text: When AIRSPY is selected as the signal source, a range of hardware-specific settings becomes available.

docs.title: Gain Mode
docs.text:
The Airspy has three gain stages one after the other: the LNA (low noise amplifier), the Mixer and - after the tuner's channel filter - the VGA (see the Gain Controls section above). The Gain Mode decides how they are set:

  • Linearity and Sensitivity are presets: a single gain value (0 - 21) sets all three stages at once, following one of two tables. They are alternatives, not two gains that add up - only the selected one is applied.
  • Manual sets LNA, Mixer and VGA gain individually.

The buttons at the top of the Gain box select the mode; below them is the slider of the selected preset, or in Manual one slider per stage.

Which preset? The two presets differ in where the gain is applied:

  • Sensitivity puts the gain into the first stages (LNA and Mixer) early. Amplifying a signal as early as possible keeps the receiver's own noise lowest, so the weakest signals come out best. But every strong signal the antenna picks up is amplified early as well, before the channel filter can remove it - with strong signals around, the first stages overload sooner.
  • Linearity keeps LNA and Mixer lower and makes up the gain with the VGA, behind the channel filter. Strong signals outside the shown band are then already attenuated when most of the gain is applied, at the cost of a little more receiver noise.

Choose Linearity when there are strong signals around: in cities, with outdoor or roof antennas, close to FM, TV or paging transmitters, and at wide sample rates - or whenever raising the gain makes the noise floor jump or "ghost" signals appear. It is the safer default. Choose Sensitivity for weak signals in a quiet environment (rural locations, small indoor antennas, satellites, narrow sample rates).

Setting the gain: raise it until the noise floor starts to rise along with it, and stop there - more gain does not make signals stand out more after that point. If the noise floor rises much faster than the signals, or wide humps and copies of strong signals appear, the receiver is overloaded: lower the gain or switch to Linearity. Values around 14 to 17 are a good start.

docs.title: Airspy HF Specific Settings
docs.text: When AIRSPYHF is selected as the signal source, a range of hardware-specific settings becomes available.

docs.title: Automatic Gain Control (AGC)
docs.text: This setting can enable the built-in AGC of the Airspy HF+. If enabled, the AGC Threshold can be set to either Low or High with a slider.

docs.title: LNA Preamp
docs.text: The Airspy HF+ includes a Low Noise Amplifier (LNA) which can be enabled with this setting. It increases the input signal level by 6dB.

docs.title: Attenuation
docs.text: If the AGC setting is turned off, an attenuation level can be chosen instead. The input signal is attenuated by a chosen factor (0 - 48dB). This is useful if strong nearby signals overload the SDR.

docs.title: HydraSDR Specific Settings
docs.text: When HYDRASDR is selected as the signal source, a range of hardware-specific settings becomes available.

docs.title: Gain Mode
docs.text: The HydraSDR has the same three gain stages (LNA, Mixer, VGA) and the same Gain Modes as the Airspy: the presets Linearity and Sensitivity (one value sets all three stages) or Manual (each stage individually). See the Airspy's Gain Mode section for how the presets differ and when to choose which.

docs.title: RF Port
docs.text:
The HydraSDR has 3 ports from which RF signals can be captured:

  • AIR_IN (also called ANT or RX0): Default antenna port
  • CABLE1 (also called RX1): First internal port
  • CABLE2 (also called RX2): Second internal port

docs.title: KiwiSDR Specific Settings
docs.text: When KiwiSDR is selected as the signal source, RF Analyzer connects to a remote KiwiSDR receiver over the network instead of using local USB hardware.

docs.title: Host / Port / Password
docs.text:
Enter the DNS Name or IP Address and Port (default 8073) of the KiwiSDR receiver. Most public KiwiSDR receivers are open and do not require a Password - leave it blank unless the receiver operator has given you one. The Password field is only editable when Secure Connection (below) is enabled, since it would otherwise be transmitted unencrypted. This must be configured before starting the analyzer.

A KiwiSDR in your own local network needs RF Analyzer's local network access on Android 17 and newer, as described for the External RTL-SDR Server.

docs.title: Secure Connection
docs.text: Most public KiwiSDR receivers only support plain (unencrypted) connections. If your receiver is known to support a secure connection (wss://, e.g. behind a TLS-terminating reverse proxy), enable Secure Connection. Otherwise, be aware that all data is sent unencrypted over the network - this is why password authentication is disabled unless this is turned on.

docs.title: Choose from Public List
docs.text: Choose from Public List opens the receivers listed on kiwisdr.com/public: a List (searchable by name, location and host, with the number of users, the HF signal-to-noise ratio and an OFFLINE badge) and a Map of the receivers around you. Tapping a receiver (on the map: Select this Receiver) fills in host and port - for a plain connection without a password - and starts the analyzer. The list is kept for an hour; Refresh loads it again.

docs.title: Sample Rate and Gain
docs.text:
A KiwiSDR covers HF (0 to 30 MHz, or what the receiver reports) and sends only a narrow slice of it: 12 kSps, about 10 kHz of usable spectrum (wideband receivers about 20 kSps). The receiver decides the rate; RF Analyzer takes it over when connected. Scroll or tune to move the slice. The receiver's own AGC sets the level, so there are no gain controls.

If the connection fails, the message says why: the receiver has no free channel slots (try another one), authentication failed, the server is down or closed the connection, or it sent no IQ stream within 15 seconds.

Be a good guest

Most KiwiSDR receivers only support 4-8 simultaneous listeners. Please be considerate of other users: don't leave the analyzer running idle against a public receiver, and disconnect (stop the analyzer) when you're done.

docs.title: File Source Settings
docs.text:
If you select File Source, you can load and replay an IQ recording. This is useful for analyzing captured signals at a later time. IQ recordings can be created via the PC software tools rtl_sdr and hackrf_transfer. RF Analyzer can also record IQ files directly (see Recordings).

Once playback has started, the tune frequency, sample rate, and file format cannot be changed. Unlike live SDR sources, an IQ file has fixed characteristics and cannot be "retuned". If these values are incorrect the recording will not be correctly replayed.

docs.title: Selecting a Source File
docs.text:
The Open File button opens a file chooser to choose an IQ file from the phone's storage. These files contain raw IQ data and no information about the file format, frequency and sample rate. Therefore, these values need to be specified after selecting the file.

Auto-Detection

When you open a file, RF Analyzer fills in frequency, sample rate and file format from its file name where it can, e.g. hackrf_123000kHz_2Msps.iq: the parts in any order, each after _, - or a space, with the units MHz, kHz or Hz and MSps, kSps or Sps. The extension .cu8, .cs8, .cs16 or .cf32 sets the format; a device name in the file name (e.g. HACKRF) wins over it. A name that starts with date and time (20261113-012148_…, as RF Analyzer names its recordings) also tells when the recording was made.

The View Recordings button lets you browse saved recordings within the app. By tapping on a recording and pressing the play button, the recording file is automatically loaded into the File Source and started. File format, frequency and sample rate do not need to be entered manually.

docs.title: Tune Frequency
docs.text:
This value sets the center frequency at which the recording was done.

Note that this frequency value is not important for the display and demodulation of the signals. It is only used to display the frequency grid. If unknown, you may set the frequency to 0Hz which is similar to enabling the Relative Frequency setting.

docs.title: Sample Rate
docs.text: This value specifies the sample rate at which the file should be replayed.

docs.title: File Format
docs.text:
The SDR devices use different file formats:

  • RTLSDR: interleaved, 8-bit, unsigned IQ samples
  • HackRF: interleaved, 8-bit, signed IQ samples
  • AIRSPY: interleaved, 16-bit, signed IQ samples
  • AIRSPYHF: interleaved, 32-bit float IQ samples (also RF Analyzer's baseband recordings and the .cf32 files of other tools)
  • HYDRASDR: interleaved, 16-bit, signed IQ samples

In all cases, the in-phase component (I) is first, followed by the quadrature component (Q).

docs.title: Repeat
docs.text: If this setting is enabled, the file will start playing again from the beginning once the end of the file is reached. It will loop forever until the Analyzer is manually stopped by the user.

docs.title: Wrapping Up
docs.text: Now that you understand the Source Tab and the FFT is running, you are ready to start exploring signals! Next, we will dive deeper into FFT & Spectrum Analysis and discuss how to interpret and optimize the FFT display.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: The Settings tab lets you customize the app's behavior to your preferences.

docs.title: Location
docs.text:
Where you listen from. RF Analyzer uses it to preselect the region of the band plans when importing default lists and to start the maps on your area.

  • Country or region - Out of the box, the country is taken from what the phone already knows, without any permission: the mobile network, the time zone, the SIM card or the language setting (shown next to the country, e.g. "from your mobile network"). Tap to choose a country yourself, only an ITU region if you'd rather not tell more, or Automatic to go back to the phone's guess.
  • Your position (optional) - The maps start there instead of on the whole country. Either type a Maidenhead grid locator (e.g. JN49 or JN49eh) - the maps draw its square as your home - or choose This device's location: RF Analyzer then asks for the approximate location permission and takes a location fix now and then while the app is open (never in the background).
Used for Country or region the region preselected when importing band plans, where the maps start Position where the maps start, the locator's square on the maps

The location stays on your device. The maps' "my location" button shows where the phone is right now, to about 2 km (RF Analyzer only asks for the approximate location), and asks for the location permission on its own, independent of this setting. If you denied it twice, Android no longer asks; the button then offers to open the app's settings, where you can allow it under Permissions → Location.

docs.title: Screen Orientation
docs.text:
By default, the AUTO setting follows your system's behavior for screen orientation. If you'd like to lock in a fixed screen orientation choose one of the following from the dropdown list:

  • Portrait
  • Landscape
  • Reverse Portrait
  • Reverse Landscape

docs.title: App Color Theme
docs.text:
This setting lets you choose the color theme of the app's controls. RF Analyzer has a standard theme but you may also choose the dynamic coloring of the Android System (available from Android Version 12):

  • RF Analyzer Theme (dark)
  • RF Analyzer Theme (light)
  • RF Analyzer Theme (system setting)
  • System Theme (dark)
  • System Theme (light)
  • System Theme (system setting)

Selecting a 'system setting' theme will use the systems' current setting for the light/dark mode. Currently RF Analyzer looks best using the RF Analyzer (dark) theme which is the default setting.

docs.title: Font Size (FFT Plot)
docs.text: The font size setting affects the size of the labels and the grid in the FFT and Waterfall plot.

docs.title: Context Help System
docs.text: This setting enables or disables the context-aware help system. If enabled, a long press on any UI element label will open the user manual section for this UI element. The label is located in the upper left gap of the border of each UI element.

docs.title: Reverse Tuning Wheel
docs.text: This checkbox allows you to reverse the direction in which the tuning wheel moves the channel indicator. The default (disabled) is that a swipe to the left on the tuning wheel also moves the channel to the left (i.e. decreasing the frequency). However, a physical tuning wheel on an old radio did actually work the other way around which can be enabled with this setting. Choose which behavior feels better or more natural for you.

docs.title: Keep Channel Centered
docs.text:
In the Settings tab, the switch Keep Channel Centered decides how the view follows the channel:

  • Enabled - The FFT display will automatically move to keep the channel selector centered when tuning to a new frequency.
  • Disabled - The FFT view remains stationary; only the channel indicator moves. If the indicator scrolls out of view, the display will then follow.

This gives you flexibility in how you want to interact with the spectrum display - either keeping the selected signal in the spotlight, or keeping a broader overview of the band.

docs.title: Start When an SDR Is Plugged In
docs.text:
If enabled, plugging in a USB SDR starts the analyzer with that SDR - also with the app in the background, which stays there, and by opening the app if it isn't running. Android asks once per SDR whether RF Analyzer may access it; tick Always open RF Analyzer when ... is connected so that plugging in works without that question.

If disabled (the default), Android doesn't offer RF Analyzer when an SDR is plugged in, so it doesn't compete with other SDR apps on your device.

docs.title: Control Drawer Alignment (Landscape)
docs.text: The Control Drawer is accessible on the side of the screen when the device is in landscape orientation. This setting lets you choose on which side the drawer should appear.

docs.title: Low Performance Mode
docs.text:
Enable only if necessary!

This mode is intended for old and less powerful devices. Only enable it if you have performance issues.

This mode reduces the quality of the filters inside the demodulation path of the app. If your demodulated audio is stuttering or choppy, it might be because your Android device is not capable at running these filters at their intended quality. In this case, enable this setting and use the filter quality slider to reduce the filter quality until the audio is not choppy anymore. Note that with reduced filter quality you will hear more noise and more importantly: you will hear aliases (think of aliases as ghost signals: they are not visible in the FFT but you can hear them in the demodulation - they are only there because the filters are too weak).

Currently, the only filter which is affected by this setting is the filter for the resampler. The resampler is used to downsample the signal from the sample rate of the SDR source (e.g. 2MHz for a RTL-SDR) to a lower sample rate for demodulation. If you enable Show Debug Information you can see the load of the resampler as percentage. If this load is greater or very close to 100%, your Android device is not able to run the filter at the necessary speed. The load on your phone increases if the input sample rate increases (e.g. with a HackRF you can go up to 20MHz) or if the number of filter taps increase. This setting reduces the filter taps to reduce the load. If possible you should rather reduce the input sample rate: This will give you better audio quality at the cost of seeing less bandwidth.

The mode also limits the drawing of the FFT and waterfall to 30 frames per second (see Max Frame Rate).

docs.title: Show Debug Information
docs.text: With this switch enabled, debug information - the frame rate and the processing load (see Processing Overload) - is printed in the upper right corner of the FFT plot.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
For debugging purposes, the app can write all log messages to a text file. Once logging is enabled, the text file can be viewed, saved to a folder, shared or deleted.

In case you encounter software errors in the app please consider giving me feedback via email (rfanalyzerapp -at- gmail.com) or via a GitHub Issue and include the log file.

In case the app crashes, please allow the Android System to collect data for a crash report. This is the most efficient way for me to be able to fix such issues.

docs.title: Wrapping Up
docs.text: This marks the end of the introduction to the RF Analyzer control drawer elements. Further information on the app (e.g. licensing and access to the manual/tutorial) can be found on the About Tab. If you are interested in further reading on signal processing and amateur radio you may head over to the Additional Information section of this manual.

docs.title: Installation & Setup
docs.text: This section explains how to install the RF Analyzer app and connect a source for RF signals. Details about the configuration of the SDR can be found in the section SDR Source.

docs.title: Installing the App
docs.text:
The app can be downloaded via the Google Play Store. Use the following link:

https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.mantz_it.rfanalyzer

You can try RF Analyzer for free for 60 minutes of operating time. A small pill above the control drawer shows the time left (for example "Trial 42m"); tap it for details. Once the time is used up, each start still runs for 30 seconds.

If you like it, a one-time in-app purchase of the Full Version unlocks it for good - no subscriptions, no accounts, no ads. Purchase options in the About tab or in the trial pill's dialog opens a sheet with its Google Play price. Purchases belong to the Google account that is active in the Play Store and come back by themselves after reinstalling or on a new phone. The About tab shows what you bought (Purchase details); Check again asks Google Play anew.

This app is a hobby project, built with passion and countless hours of work. Supporting the app helps me continue developing and improving it. Thank you! 🙏

docs.title: Drivers
docs.text: No driver app is needed: RF Analyzer has built-in drivers for every supported SDR - RTL-SDR, HackRF, Airspy, Airspy HF+ and HydraSDR. (Up to version 2.2, the RTL-SDR needed the separate "RTL2832U driver" app; it is no longer used and can be uninstalled.)

docs.title: SDRs via USB
docs.text:
The SDR is connected via USB to your Android device using a USB OTG adapter. You might have received such an adapter with your phone as it is usually used to transfer data from your old phone to the new one.

When the analyzer starts with the SDR for the first time, Android asks whether RF Analyzer may access the USB device. Check Always open RF Analyzer when … is connected if you don't want to be asked each time.

RF Analyzer selects the matching source type by itself when an SDR is plugged in while the app is open (or when you return to the app after plugging it in). With Start When an SDR Is Plugged In in the Settings tab, plugging it in also starts the analyzer.

docs.title: RTL-SDR via TCP
docs.text:
The RTL-SDR can be set up on a computer and accessed/operated via the network. On your host computer, execute rtl_tcp to start a SDR server. The following command line starts the server on TCP port 4242 assuming the IP address of your host is 192.168.0.42:

rtl_tcp -a 192.168.0.42 -p 4242

Select RTLSDR in the Source tab, enable External Server (rtl_tcp) and enter the server's DNS Name / IP Address and Port. Then start the analyzer with the Play button. On Android 17 and newer, a server in your own network needs RF Analyzer's local network permission (see External RTL-SDR Server).

Firewall might block access to the server

If your host computer is behind a firewall or has a local firewall installed, RF Analyzer might not be able to connect to the port. In this case, add an exception to the firewall to allow incoming traffic to the port specified in rtl_tcp.

docs.title: KiwiSDR Web Receivers (No Hardware Needed)
docs.text: Select KiwiSDR (web) in the Source tab and tap Choose from Public List: pick a receiver from the list or the map, and the analyzer starts. All you need is an internet connection. See KiwiSDR for details.

docs.title: File Source (Playback of Recordings and IQ Files)
docs.text:
RF Analyzer plays back IQ files in these formats (in-phase I first, then quadrature Q):

  • RTLSDR: 8-bit unsigned (.cu8, e.g. from rtl_sdr)
  • HACKRF: 8-bit signed (.cs8, e.g. from hackrf_transfer -r)
  • AIRSPY / HYDRASDR: 16-bit signed (.cs16)
  • AIRSPYHF: 32-bit float (.cf32, also RF Analyzer's baseband recordings)

Select File Source in the Source tab, then Open File for a file from storage or View Recordings for one of your recordings.
